timeline.title: Born at Woolsthorpe
timeline.text: Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe Manor, a farmhouse in Lincolnshire. England then used the old Julian calendar, which records his birth as Christmas Day, 25 December 1642. By today's Gregorian calendar it was 4 January 1643. His father, also named Isaac, had died about three months before.

timeline.title: Raised by his grandmother
timeline.text: When he was three, his mother Hannah married the Reverend Barnabas Smith and went to live with him, leaving Isaac in the care of his grandmother, Margery Ayscough.

timeline.title: School in Grantham
timeline.text: From about 12 to 17 he attended the King's School in Grantham. William Stukeley later wrote that he was skilled with tools and covered his room's walls with drawings of birds, ships and mathematical figures.

timeline.title: Called home to farm
timeline.text: His mother, widowed again, took him out of school to run the farm. He was not suited to it. His schoolmaster and an uncle persuaded her to send him back to school.

timeline.title: Trinity College
timeline.text: He was admitted to Trinity College, Cambridge, as a subsizar, a poorer student who paid his way partly by working as a servant. In 1664 he won a scholarship.

timeline.title: Degree, then plague
timeline.text: He took his BA. Soon after, the university closed because of the Great Plague, and he went home to Woolsthorpe.

timeline.title: The years of wonders
timeline.text: Working alone at home between 1665 and 1667, he developed early ideas on calculus (which he called fluxions), optics and gravity. An October 1666 manuscript records his calculus.

timeline.title: Fellow of Trinity
timeline.text: Back in Cambridge from April, he was elected a fellow of Trinity College in October.

timeline.title: The reflecting telescope
timeline.text: Late in 1668 he built a telescope that used a curved mirror instead of a lens, to avoid the coloured blur that lenses cause. Its mirror was only about 33 mm across.

timeline.title: Lucasian Professor
timeline.text: At 26 he succeeded his teacher Isaac Barrow as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, and lectured on optics.

timeline.title: Royal Society and light
timeline.text: A second telescope was shown to King Charles II in January. Newton was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and published his paper on white light being made of colours. Criticism of it, including from Robert Hooke, led to long and bitter arguments.

timeline.title: On the shoulders of giants
timeline.text: In a letter to Hooke dated 5 February 1675 by the old calendar (1676 by ours), Newton wrote that if he had seen further it was by standing on the shoulders of giants. The image was centuries old, going back to Bernard of Chartres.

timeline.title: Halley's question
timeline.text: The astronomer Edmond Halley visited, probably in August, to ask about planetary orbits. In November Newton sent him a short paper, De motu corporum in gyrum (On the motion of bodies in orbit). It grew into the Principia.

timeline.title: Hooke's claim
timeline.text: Hooke claimed he had found the inverse-square law of gravity first. He could not support the claim, but it caused delay and anger. Samuel Pepys licensed the book for printing on 30 June.

timeline.title: The Principia
timeline.text: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published, with Halley paying the costs at his own risk. It set out the three laws of motion and universal gravitation.

timeline.title: Member of Parliament
timeline.text: He served as Member of Parliament for Cambridge University in 1689-1690, and again in 1701-1702.

timeline.title: A year of crisis
timeline.text: A close friendship ended suddenly, and Newton went through a period of deep distress, sending accusing letters to his friends Samuel Pepys and John Locke.

timeline.title: Warden of the Mint
timeline.text: He moved to London to run the Royal Mint during the Great Recoinage. He hunted counterfeiters himself, carrying out over 100 cross-examinations and prosecuting 28 coiners. In 1699 he became Master of the Mint, a post he held until his death.

timeline.title: President of the Royal Society
timeline.text: He became President of the Royal Society, and held the post until 1727. Hooke died the same year.

timeline.title: Opticks
timeline.text: He published Opticks in English, a book built on experiments with light and colour. He had held it back until after Hooke's death. It ended with open questions, the Queries, which grew in later editions.

timeline.title: Knighted
timeline.text: Queen Anne knighted him during a royal visit to Trinity College. He was the second scientist to be knighted, after Francis Bacon.

timeline.title: The calculus quarrel
timeline.text: A bitter dispute raged over whether Newton or the German thinker Gottfried Leibniz had invented calculus. A Royal Society committee ruled for Newton, but it never heard Leibniz's side and Newton wrote the report himself. Historians today agree both men invented it independently. Sources date the report to 1712 or early 1713.

timeline.title: Principia, second edition
timeline.text: A revised Principia, edited by Roger Cotes, added the General Scholium, where Newton wrote that he would 'frame no hypotheses' about the cause of gravity.

timeline.title: The South Sea Bubble
timeline.text: When the South Sea Company's shares collapsed, Newton lost at least 10,000 pounds and perhaps more than 20,000.

timeline.title: The apple story
timeline.text: Newton told his friend William Stukeley that the idea of gravity came to him when an apple fell in the garden at Woolsthorpe. This is an anecdote Stukeley wrote down later, in a 1752 memoir, not a record from the 1660s. Voltaire spread the story from 1727.

timeline.title: Death in Kensington
timeline.text: Newton died on 20 March 1727 by the old calendar (31 March by ours). He was buried in Westminster Abbey on 28 March (old calendar), the first scientist given that honour.

timeline.title: The Principia in English
timeline.text: Andrew Motte published the first English translation of the Principia, from the 1726 third edition.

timeline.title: The monument in the Abbey
timeline.text: His monument by Michael Rysbrack, designed by William Kent, was unveiled in Westminster Abbey. Alexander Pope's famous epitaph, 'Let Newton be! and all was light', was not allowed on it.

works.title: Calculus (fluxions)
works.text: A method for working with change and motion, recorded in an October 1666 manuscript but not published until 1737. Leibniz found it independently.

works.title: The reflecting telescope
works.text: A telescope using a mirror instead of a lens, free of the colour blur lenses produce. The design is still called the Newtonian telescope.

works.title: Paper on white light and colours
works.text: His paper to the Royal Society arguing that white light is a mixture of colours.

works.title: De motu corporum in gyrum
works.text: A short paper for Halley on how bodies move in orbits, the seed of the Principia.

works.title: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
works.text: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy: the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, explaining both falling bodies and planets.

works.title: Three laws of motion
works.text: Bodies keep moving or stay at rest unless a force acts; force changes motion; every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

works.title: Universal gravitation
works.text: Every body attracts every other, with a force that weakens with the square of the distance.

works.title: The Royal Mint
works.text: As Warden and then Master of the Mint, he oversaw the recoinage and pursued counterfeiters.

works.title: Opticks
works.text: His book of experiments on light and colour, written in English and ending with his famous Queries.

works.title: General Scholium
works.text: The closing essay added to the Principia's second edition, on method and on God, where he refused to guess the cause of gravity.

works.title: Alchemy and theology papers
works.text: Over half of his writing dealt with alchemy and religion, most never printed in his lifetime. The Newton Project is publishing it all online.

works.title: The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended
works.text: A revised dating of the ancient world, published after his death; part of the large body of writing he did outside physics.
